concepts.title: Sociology and the Need to Unlearn Common Sense
concepts.definition: Sociology is the one subject nobody starts from zero, since everyone grows up knowing something about society, but this very familiarity is a handicap: common sense is learned from one's own social group and environment, so it is partial in both senses -- incomplete, showing only a slice of social reality, and biased, tilted towards one's own group's interests -- and the first job of learning sociology is therefore to unlearn what seems obvious.
concepts.key_idea: What feels like natural knowledge about society is really the viewpoint of the group we were socialised into, and sociology begins by doubting it.
question_patterns: why is prior knowledge of society both an advantage and a disadvantage for sociology
what does it mean to unlearn common sense in sociology
explain the two senses in which common sense knowledge is partial
how does our social context shape our beliefs about society
why does sociology feel easy to students at first
distinguish sociological knowledge from common sense knowledge

solution_steps.explain: no child needs to be taught that society exists; even a six year old knows something about social relationships, so students rarely fear the subject
opinions, beliefs and expectations are acquired from the viewpoint of the social group and environment that socialised us
because our knowledge is incomplete and tilted toward our own group, the initial stage of sociology consists mainly of unlearning this common sense

worked_examples.q: Common sense is learned from one's own social group, so it is partial or complete?

concepts.title: Self-Reflexivity: Looking at Yourself from the Outside
concepts.definition: Sociology can show you what you look like to others: self-reflexivity is the ability to turn back the gaze that is usually directed outward and inspect yourself critically -- quick to criticise and slow to praise oneself -- so that the sociologist becomes an object of study along with society.
concepts.key_idea: The sociologist's first field of observation is the sociologist's own standpoint.
question_patterns: what is meant by self reflexivity in sociology
why must self inspection in sociology be critical
how can sociology teach you to look at yourself from the outside
distinguish the outward gaze from the reflexive gaze
why is reflexivity important for controlling the bias of common sense
explain reflexivity as a skill of the sociological temperament

solution_steps.explain: self-reflexivity is the capacity to reflect upon yourself and turn the gaze normally pointed at others back toward yourself
the self-inspection must be quick to criticise and slow to praise oneself, otherwise it merely repeats the biases of one's group
reflexivity complements unlearning common sense by exposing the observer's own social location

worked_examples.q: Turning the outward gaze back and inspecting yourself critically is called what?

concepts.title: The Social Map: Locating Individuals in Society
concepts.definition: Every person occupies a position on a social map made of overlapping group memberships: as a seventeen or eighteen year old you belong to the young people who form roughly forty per cent of India's population, you may carry a regional or linguistic identity such as Gujarati or Telugu speaker, an economic class from your family's income and occupation, and a religion, caste or tribe -- each identity placing you in a web of social relationships whose patterns sociology describes and connects.
concepts.formula: social_map = age_group + region_and_language + economic_class + religion + caste_or_tribe
concepts.key_idea: Who you are socially is a set of coordinates on many maps at once, and sociology reads the whole atlas.
question_patterns: what kinds of groups locate a person on the social map
why are young people described as a large social group in india
how do class and caste place an individual in society differently
explain the idea of a web of social relationships
what does sociology tell us beyond describing social groups
how would you locate yourself on a social map of india

solution_steps.explain: age group, region and language, economic class, religion and caste or tribe together fix a person's location on the social map

solution_steps.action: verify the demographic weight of youth
solution_steps.explain: people of seventeen or eighteen and younger account for about forty per cent of India's population, making youth a major social grouping
sociology identifies the groupings, explains their relationships to one another and draws out what these mean for individual lives

worked_examples.q: Young people form roughly what percent of India's population?

concepts.title: Personal Troubles and Social Issues: Mills's Distinction
concepts.definition: C. Wright Mills shows that sociology connects personal troubles and social issues: a trouble is the worry, problem or concern of a single individual -- family treatment, friendship strains, anxiety about a future job -- and derives meaning from a personalised perspective, while an issue concerns large groups rather than the individuals composing them, so sociology maps the links between the two levels.
concepts.key_idea: What feels like a private worry is often the individual end of a public issue, and mapping that link is sociology's special skill.
question_patterns: distinguish between personal troubles and social issues
what did c wright mills mean by mapping links between troubles and issues
give an example of a personal trouble that points to a social issue
why are social issues about groups rather than individuals
how does the sociological imagination connect biography and society
classify unemployment anxiety as a trouble or an issue and justify

solution_steps.explain: individual worries about family treatment, siblings, friends or future employment are troubles belonging to one person's perspective
an issue concerns large groups -- say the whole cohort of job seekers -- and cannot be explained by one biography alone
sociology traces the connections so that private experience is read against the group pattern it belongs to

worked_examples.q: Which sociologist distinguished personal troubles from social issues: C. Wright Mills or Malthus?

concepts.title: A Preview of the Book: Processes Shaping Indian Society
concepts.definition: The introduction sketches the ground ahead: demographic structure of a population soon to be the world's largest; the institutions of caste, tribe and family that form the basic building blocks; the market as a socio-cultural vehicle of change from colonialism to developmental policy; the patterns of inequality and exclusion around caste, tribe, gender and the disabled; the hard side of unity in diversity with communal conflict, regional and linguistic chauvinism and casteism; and finally practical project work for doing sociological research oneself.
concepts.formula: structure_of_indian_society = demography + caste_tribe_family + market + inequality_and_exclusion + diversity_challenges
concepts.key_idea: The syllabus of Indian society runs from population, through institutions and the market, to inequality, diversity and hands-on research.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy101.txt 1.2 A Preview of this Book (lines 76-138)
question_patterns: give an outline of the main themes of the textbook on indian society
why is caste described as a unique feature of the indian subcontinent
what questions does the study of demographic structure raise
how is the market treated as a vehicle of change in indian history
which groups does the chapter on inequality and exclusion focus on
why must every minority in india not feel insecure for the nation's future

solution_steps.explain: chapters on demography and on caste, tribe and family establish the population base and the building blocks of society

solution_steps.action: verify the change and conflict agenda
solution_steps.explain: the market chapter traces chain reactions from colonialism to development policy, and the inequality chapter follows caste, tribe, gender and the disabled

solution_steps.action: verify the diversity and practice agenda
solution_steps.explain: the diversity chapter weighs strengths and weaknesses against communalism, chauvinism and casteism, and the final chapter opens small practical research projects

worked_examples.q: Which basic institutions form the building blocks of Indian society: caste, tribe and family, or banks and malls?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student worries she may not get a job after school. How would Mills have us re-read this worry?

solution_template.explain: anxiety about one's own future employment is a trouble belonging to one individual's perspective
read against the group, the worry points to the situation of her whole age cohort in the job market
sociology links the private anxiety to the public pattern of unemployment, converting biography into a window on society

worked_examples.question_pattern: Name the social coordinates that locate a Telugu-speaking eighteen year old from an upper class family on India's social map.

solution_template.explain: as a member of the young people, a group forming about forty per cent of the population
regional and linguistic community -- a Telugu speaker of Andhra Pradesh

solution_template.action: fix the class and community coordinates
solution_template.explain: economic class from parental occupation and family income, plus any religious, caste or tribe membership, completing the position in the web of social relationships
